Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment

Mingxuan Li, Kai-Zhan Lee, Elias Bareinboim

Keywords: temporal credit assignment, counterfactual Shapley values, causal inference

Abstract

The Credit Assignment Problem (CAP) is fundamental to developing efficient and explainable Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. Existing frameworks, whether relying on temporal contiguity or hindsight-conditioned reweighting of rewards, frequently fail to distribute credit properly between an agent’s policy (skill) and environmental stochasticity (luck). A principled approach to the CAP must isolate the causes of observed rewards from spurious correlated features and environmental randomness. We introduce Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment, a novel causal credit assignment framework based on the counterfactual Shapley value (ϕ\phi-value). By redistributing rewards, ϕ\phi-values enhance credit assignment across three critical dimensions: high stochasticity, sparse causality, and delayed rewards, all while theoretically preserving the original optimal policy. We derive a consistent estimator that computes each ϕ\phi-value in amortized constant time complexity, enabling a new class of policy gradient methods, ϕ\phi-PPO. Empirical results demonstrate that ϕ\phi-values align precisely with the ground truth causes of task rewards. Furthermore, we show its superior sample efficiency in challenging environments where prior state-of-the-art methods fail to converge.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) agents have achieved remarkable success in domains such as healthcare (Yu et al., 2020), autonomous driving (Shao et al., 2019), and code generation (Anthropic, 2024; Yang et al., 2025), driven by advances in deep RL (Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2017; OpenAI et al., 2019; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Guo et al., 2025). As RL scales to more challenging domains with longer horizons, sparse and delayed rewards, and greater stochasticity, the long-standing Credit Assignment Problem (CAP) grows increasingly relevant: learning depends on successfully “distributing credit for success of a complex strategy among the many decisions that were involved” (Minsky, 1961). We argue that this credit distribution must be causal: the credit each action receives should reflect its causal effect on the total discounted reward.

However, locating the true causes of the rewards is challenging (Pignatelli et al., 2024). In Figure 1, we construct a simple MDP to reflect this intricate nature of CAP. Under a uniform random policy, the agent’s first action determines which branch it follows. On the top branch, the last action determines the reward: one choice yields reward 11 with certainty (“Skill,” red) while the other yields 00 (gray). On the bottom branch, the reward is 00 or 11 with equal probability regardless of the last action (“Luck,” blue). Thus, a good credit assignment method should assign bigger positive credit to both the first and last actions on Skill trajectory than those on Luck, since changing either one would have altered the return distribution. On the Luck trajectory, the last action has no causal effect on the return and should receive zero credit. Surprisingly, as we show in Figure 1, none of the prominent existing methods produces the fully correct credit assignment (see Appendix G for a detailed discussion).

Humans, on the other hand, routinely perform credit assignment which does not seem to be challenging as it appears to machines. One possible reason is that we are endowed with causal reasoning capabilities that enable us to allocate credit counterfactually. Chess masters, for instance, replay key positions after every game, analyzing what would have happened under different moves. As Kasparov (2007) writes, “it is so important to question success as vigorously as you question failure.” Structural causal models (SCMs) (Pearl, 2009; Bareinboim et al., 2022) formalize this type of counterfactual reasoning: given an observed trajectory, we can simulate the outcome under a different action at any step while holding all other factors fixed, isolating the causal effect of that decision. This type of counterfactual analysis lays the foundation for a fine-grained attribution for individual actions in each trajectory regardless of delayed effect, stochasticity and sparsity of the reward signals.

In this work, building on the Counterfactual Shapley Value (ϕ\phi-value) framework of Lee et al. (2025), we distribute the total causal effect across actions using Shapley values (Shapley, 1953), which provide the unique allocation satisfying efficiency, symmetry, and null-player axioms. The resulting ϕ\phi-MDP replaces the environment’s reward signal with per-step ϕ\phi-values, providing dense causal learning signals even when the original reward is delayed or sparse. We prove this redistribution preserves the optimal policy (Theorem 3.7) and derive a consistent estimator computing all TT values from a single coalition sample in O⁡(T)O(T) time (Theorem 4.2). We integrate these into ϕ\phi-PPO, which replaces per-step rewards with ϕ\phi-values and uses Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR). PTR selects subtrajectories by causal importance, in contrast to PER (Schaul et al., 2015b) which prioritizes individual transitions by TD error. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    Credit Assignment via ϕ\phi-values. We show that credit assignment via ϕ\phi-values is equivalent to a reward redistribution that preserves the optimal policy and spikes only on causal actions.

  • •

    Tractable ϕ\phi-value Estimation. We propose a consistent ϕ\phi-value estimator that achieves linear time complexity, with a tunable bias–variance tradeoff via λ\lambda-bootstrapping.

  • •

    Efficient and Explainable Policy Optimization. We propose ϕ\phi-PPO and demonstrate its strong empirical performance in several challenging credit assignment testbeds.

2 Preliminaries

In this section, we establish foundational concepts to facilitate our discussion. Throughout the paper, we use uppercase letters to denote random variables (XX), lowercase for their realizations (xx) and bold letters for sets (𝐕\mathbf{V}).

2.1 Structural Causal Models and MDPs

Structural Causal Models (SCMs) lay the mathematical foundations for counterfactual reasoning needed to isolate causal contributions (Bareinboim et al., 2022).

Definition 2.1 (Structural Causal Model).

An SCM is ℳ=⟨𝐕,𝐔,ℱ,P⁡(𝐔)⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathbf{V},\mathbf{U},\mathcal{F},P(\mathbf{U})\rangle where 𝐕\mathbf{V} is endogenous variables, 𝐔\mathbf{U} is exogenous variables, ℱ={fi}\mathcal{F}=\{f_{i}\} are structural equations Vi=fi​(𝐏𝐚i,𝐔i)V_{i}=f_{i}(\mathbf{Pa}_{i},\mathbf{U}_{i}), and P⁡(𝐔)P(\mathbf{U}) is exogenous distribution.

Under this definition, the counterfactual V𝐱​(𝐮)V_{\mathbf{x}}(\mathbf{u}) is the value of VV when 𝐗\mathbf{X} is set to 𝐱\mathbf{x} while 𝐔=𝐮\mathbf{U}=\mathbf{u}. Then we cast MDPs as SCMs to ground the credit assignment discussion with causal semantics.

Definition 2.2 (MDP-SCM).

An MDP-SCM is an SCM with endogenous variables 𝐕={St,Xt,Yt}t=1T∪{Y}\mathbf{V}=\{S_{t},X_{t},Y_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T}\cup\{Y\} (states, actions, per-step rewards, and outcome Y=fY(Y1:T)Y=f_{Y}(Y_{1:T})), mutually independent exogenous variables 𝐔={USt,UXt,UYt}t=1T\mathbf{U}=\{U_{S_{t}},U_{X_{t}},U_{Y_{t}}\}_{t=1}^{T}, and structural equations defining system dynamics: S1=fS​(US1),St+1=fS​(St,Xt,USt+1),Xt=π⁡(St,UXt),Yt=r⁡(St,Xt,UYt)S_{1}=f_{S}(U_{S_{1}}),S_{t+1}=f_{S}(S_{t},X_{t},U_{S_{t+1}}),X_{t}=\pi(S_{t},U_{X_{t}}),\ Y_{t}=r(S_{t},X_{t},U_{Y_{t}}).

We use P⁡(S)P(S) to denote the initial state distribution induced by US1U_{S_{1}} and the discounted total reward as the outcome Y=∑tγt−1​YtY=\sum_{t}\gamma^{t-1}Y_{t}. Value functions V⁡(s)V(s), Q-values Q⁡(s,x)Q(s,x), and advantages A⁡(s,x)A(s,x) under MDP-SCM follow the standard RL definitions (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Sec. 3.1).

2.2 Policy Gradients

The goal of reinforcement learning is to find the policy that maximizes the cumulative reward (outcome), π∗=arg⁡maxπ​𝔼τ∼ℳπ​[Y],\pi^{*}=\arg\max_{\pi}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathcal{M}^{\pi}}[Y], where trajectory τ∼ℳπ\tau\sim\mathcal{M}^{\pi} is sampled from the environment MDP ℳπ\mathcal{M}^{\pi} under policy π\pi. Optimizing this objective with respect to a parameterized policy πθ\pi_{\theta} leads to the basic form of policy gradients (Williams, 1992),

𝔼⁡[∑t≥0γt​∇θ​log⁡π⁡(xt|st)​(∑t′≥tγt′−t​Yt′−V⁡(st))]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi(x_{t}|s_{t})\big(\sum_{t^{\prime}\geq t}\gamma^{t^{\prime}-t}Y_{t^{\prime}}-V(s_{t})\big)\Big] (1)

where V⁡(st)=𝔼⁡[∑t′≥tγt′−t​Yt′|st]V(s_{t})=\mathbb{E}\big[\sum_{t^{\prime}\geq t}\gamma^{t^{\prime}-t}Y_{t^{\prime}}|s_{t}\big] is the value function. Here it serves as a baseline with respect to which the advantage of taking the specific action xtx_{t} instead of others is strengthened. Subtracting the baseline will not bias the gradient as long as the baseline is a function of state sts_{t}. Modern policy gradient methods use generalized advantages (Schulman et al., 2016) and gradient clipping (Schulman et al., 2017) to reduce variance. In this work, we base our learning algorithm on proximal policy gradient (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), whose objective is to maximize the following,

min⁡(rt​(θ)​A^t,clip⁡(rt​(θ),1−ϵclip,1+ϵclip)​A^t)\displaystyle\min\bigl(r_{t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{t},\;\mathrm{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1{-}\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1{+}\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})\hat{A}_{t}\bigr) (2)

where A^t=∑ℓ=0T−t+1(γ​λ)ℓ​δt+ℓ,δt=Yt+γ​V​(st+1)−V⁡(st)\hat{A}_{t}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T-t+1}(\gamma\lambda)^{\ell}\delta_{t+\ell},\ \delta_{t}=Y_{t}+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_{t}) is the generalized advantage and rt​(θ)=πθ​(xt|st)πθold​(xt|st)r_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(x_{t}|s_{t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\operatorname{old}}}(x_{t}|s_{t})} is the importance ratio between the current policy distribution and the previous policy collecting the data.

2.3 Counterfactual Shapley Values

Shapley values (Shapley and others, 1953) fairly distribute credit among players in cooperative games. Given players 𝐗\mathbf{X} and value function f:2𝐗→ℝf:2^{\mathbf{X}}\to\mathbb{R}, a coalition 𝐙⊆𝐗\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{X} is a subset of players, and f⁡(𝐙)f(\mathbf{Z}) measures their joint contribution. The Shapley value ϕt\phi_{t} quantifies player XtX_{t}’s fair share of the total value f⁡(𝐗)−f⁡(∅)f(\mathbf{X})-f(\emptyset):

ϕt=∑𝐙⊆𝐗∖{Xt}|𝐙|!​(T−|𝐙|−1)!T!​[f⁡(𝐙∪{Xt})−f⁡(𝐙)].\displaystyle\phi_{t}=\sum_{\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X_{t}\}}\frac{|\mathbf{Z}|!(T-|\mathbf{Z}|-1)!}{T!}\bigl[f(\mathbf{Z}\cup\{X_{t}\})-f(\mathbf{Z})\bigr]. (3)

Shapley values satisfy desirable properties (Shapley and others, 1953), including efficiency: ∑tϕt=f⁡(𝐗)−f⁡(∅)\sum_{t}\phi_{t}=f(\mathbf{X})-f(\emptyset). For credit assignment, actions 𝐗={X1,…,XT}\mathbf{X}=\{X_{1},\ldots,X_{T}\} are players, and given trajectory τ=(s1:T,x1:T,y1:T)\tau=(s_{1:T},x_{1:T},y_{1:T}) (the evidence for counterfactual reasoning), the Shapley value ϕt\phi_{t} quantifies how much XtX_{t} contributed to outcome YY.

Causal Contributions.

We use counterfactual natural total effect (Lee et al., 2025) to measure a set of actions’ causal contributions to the outcome. It is the expected difference between the observed outcome and a counterfactual outcome where a subset of actions are replaced. “Natural” means the comparison uses the posterior P⁡(𝐔∣τ)P(\mathbf{U}\mid\tau) rather than the prior, ensuring the counterfactual is consistent with the observed trajectory:

f⁡(𝐙)\displaystyle f(\mathbf{Z}) =NTE⁡(𝐙,Y∣τ)=𝔼𝐮′∼P⁡(𝐔),𝐮∼P⁡(𝐔∣τ)​[Y⁡(𝐮)−Y𝐙⁡(𝐮′)​(𝐮)],\displaystyle=\mathrm{NTE}(\mathbf{Z},Y\mid\tau)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{u^{\prime}}\sim P(\mathbf{U}),\mathbf{u}\sim P(\mathbf{U}\mid\tau)\end{subarray}}\bigl[Y(\mathbf{u})-Y_{\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{u}^{\prime})}(\mathbf{u})\bigr], (4)

where Y⁡(𝐮)Y(\mathbf{u}) is the observed outcome and Y𝐙⁡(𝐮′)​(𝐮)Y_{\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{u}^{\prime})}(\mathbf{u}) is the counterfactual with coalition actions replaced by baseline alternatives 𝐙⁡(𝐮′)\mathbf{Z}(\mathbf{u}^{\prime}) sampled from a baseline policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} (Sec. 3.1), while exogenous 𝐮\mathbf{u} is fixed.

Kernel Formulation.

The standard Shapley formula sums over T!T! permutations; the kernel formulation (Lundberg and Lee, 2017) sums over 2T2^{T} coalitions, enabling amortization (Section 4). Let 𝐳∈{0,1}T\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{T} denote the coalition mask (zt=1z_{t}=1 iff Xt∈𝐙X_{t}\in\mathbf{Z}):

ϕt=∑𝐳∈{0,1}Tκt​(𝐳)⋅f⁡(𝐳),\phi_{t}=\sum_{\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{T}}\kappa_{t}(\mathbf{z})\cdot f(\mathbf{z}), (5)

where |𝐳|=∑tzt|\mathbf{z}|=\sum_{t}z_{t} and κt​(𝐳)=1T​(T−1|𝐳|−1)\kappa_{t}(\mathbf{z})=\frac{1}{T\binom{T-1}{|\mathbf{z}|-1}} if zt=1z_{t}=1 while κt​(𝐳)=−1T​(T−1|𝐳|)\kappa_{t}(\mathbf{z})=-\frac{1}{T\binom{T-1}{|\mathbf{z}|}} if zt=0z_{t}=0.

3 Counterfactual Credit Assignment

In the remainder of the text, we introduce our proposed causal solution to CAP. In Section 3, we formalize the credit assignment problem from a causal perspective, propose ϕ\phi-values as a principled solution and its related calculations in the RL context. In Section 4, we develop efficient estimators for ϕ\phi-values and incorporate them into policy learning. Figure 2 visualizes the conceptual structures.

First, we define the Credit Assignment Problem (CAP) as a causal inference problem: only actions that causally contribute to the outcome should receive credit, proportional to their contributions.

Definition 3.1 (Causal Credit Assignment, Informal).

A causal credit assignment function is a mapping ϕ\phi that maps a trajectory, an action at a time step and a baseline policy to a real number denoting its causal contribution to the outcome observed in the trajectory,

ϕ:τ×𝒳×T×Π↦ℝT\displaystyle\phi:\tau\times\mathcal{X}\times T\times\Pi\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{T} (6)

where τ∼ℳπ\tau\sim\mathcal{M}_{\pi} is a trajectory sampled from the baseline policy and Π\Pi is the policy space. The causal assignment ϕ\phi should satisfy the following desiderata,

  1. 𝐃1\mathbf{D}_{1}

    Causal Admissibility : Non-cause actions should be assigned zero credit;

  2. 𝐃2\mathbf{D}_{2}

    Causal Power : Actions causing the rewards should be assigned non-zero credit;

  3. 𝐃3\mathbf{D}_{3}

    Causal Normality : Actions against more probable baseline policies get more credit;

  4. 𝐃4\mathbf{D}_{4}

    Causal Effect Scaling : Given the same baseline policy, actions affecting the outcome more should be allocated more credit.

A complete formal version of the causal credit assignment desiderata is presented in App. C, Def. C.3. Here, we measure each action’s causal contribution to the outcome as the counterfactual natural total effect (Eq. 4). Unlike discounted summation of rewards, the counterfactual natural total effect is the difference between the returns under baseline policy and returns had we acted differently given an already realized trajectory. Advantage function shares a similar idea but they cannot capture counterfactual outcomes with respect to specific trajectories or quantify an action’s full potential under different action selections at other time steps.

Counterfactual natural total effect provides a fair source of credit pool as the basis for allocation and these desiderata are axioms embedded in human credit assignment systems, which a causal credit assignment function should satisfy. 𝐃𝟏,𝐃𝟐\mathbf{D_{1},D_{2}} together guarantee that the credit assignment function generates both sufficient and necessary allocations. That is, actions get credit if and only if they cause the outcome. 𝐃𝟑,𝐃𝟒\mathbf{D_{3},D_{4}} require that the scale of the allocated credit should reflect an action’s relative contribution compared against a baseline policy. We show that counterfactual Shapley values (ϕ\phi-values, Eq. 5) calculated from counterfactual natural total effect satisfy the above desiderata (Lee et al., 2025) and is a desirable credit assignment method.

Theorem 3.2 (ϕ\phi-Values are Causal).

ϕ\phi-values satisfy the causal credit assignment criteria, 𝐃𝟏−𝐃𝟒\mathbf{D_{1}-D_{4}}.

Next, we present the details in calculating ϕ\phi-values and ϕ\phi-MDP, an MDP that redistributes rewards according to Counterfactual Shapley values, as our solution to the Causal Credit Assignment Problem.

3.1 Counterfactual Simulation

To compute Shapley values ϕt\phi_{t}, we need a causal contribution function f:2𝐗→ℝf:2^{\mathbf{X}}\to\mathbb{R} measuring 𝐗\mathbf{X}’s contribution under a given coalition 𝐳\mathbf{z}. The NTE from Section 2.3 averages over both posterior and prior exogenous variables; here, we condition on the observed trajectory, giving the conditional causal contribution: f⁡(𝐳)=Y−Yσ𝐳,f(\mathbf{z})=Y-Y_{\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}}, where YY is the observed return and Yσ𝐳Y_{\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}} is the counterfactual return under intervention σ𝐳\sigma_{\mathbf{z}} which specifies counterfactual actions based on coalition membership 𝐳∈{0,1}T\mathbf{z}\in\{0,1\}^{T} and trajectory state:

σ𝐳​(t)={xtzt=0,st𝐳=stx∼π(⋅∣s𝐳t)zt=0,st𝐳≠stx∼πbase(⋅∣s𝐳t)zt=1\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}(t)=\begin{cases}x_{t}&z_{t}=0,\ s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=s_{t}\\ x\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t})&z_{t}=0,\ s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\neq s_{t}\\ x\sim\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\cdot\mid s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t})&z_{t}=1\end{cases} (7)

where st𝐳s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t} is the counterfactual state at time tt. The baseline πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} defines the “default” actions for intervened time steps. Options include: uniform random (πbase​(x∣s)=1/|𝒜|\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(x\mid s)=1/|\mathcal{A}|), measuring contribution relative to random behavior; a fixed reference policy π0\pi_{0}, measuring improvement over π0\pi_{0}; or self-baseline (πbase=π\pi_{\mathrm{base}}=\pi), isolating whether the specific action xtx_{t} matters versus what the same policy typically does. We use self-baseline throughout training (Section 5.3 illustrates the effect of alternative baselines on attributions). The intervention design rests on the following assumption.

Assumption 3.3 (Counterfactual Independence).

Exogenous noise is independent across steps: (St+1)St,Xt⟂(St+1)St′,Xt′(S_{t+1})_{S_{t},X_{t}}\perp(S_{t+1})_{S^{\prime}_{t},X^{\prime}_{t}} for (St,Xt)≠(St′,Xt′)(S_{t},X_{t})\neq(S^{\prime}_{t},X^{\prime}_{t}), and (Xt)St⟂(Xt)St′(X_{t})_{S_{t}}\perp(X_{t})_{S^{\prime}_{t}} for St≠St′S_{t}\neq S^{\prime}_{t}.

This assumption does not constrain the MDP, only its SCM representation. Since any distribution can be sampled via inverse CDF with independent uniform noise, any MDP admits an SCM with independent exogenous variables and the same optimal policy; the assumption selects this representation. The consequence is simple: when parents match the observed trajectory, the observed value is the counterfactual; when parents differ, we resample. For actions (parent StS_{t}): when zt=0z_{t}=0 and st𝐳=sts^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=s_{t}, the counterfactual equals the observed xtx_{t}; when st𝐳≠sts^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}\neq s_{t}, we resample from π(⋅∣st𝐳)\pi(\cdot\mid s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}). When zt=1z_{t}=1, we resample from πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}. For transitions and rewards (parents (St,Xt)(S_{t},X_{t})): when (st𝐳,xt𝐳)=(st,xt)(s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t},x^{\mathbf{z}}_{t})=(s_{t},x_{t}), we reuse (st+1,yt)(s_{t+1},y_{t}); otherwise, we resample. See Fig. 3 for a visualization of the counterfactual simulation process.

The full pseudo-code is provided in Algo. 2 in appendix Sec. A; Section 4 makes exact computation tractable via coalition sampling.

3.2 Reward Redistribution

With the counterfactual Shapley values, we can define a new rewarding system based on ϕt\phi_{t} while keeping the system dynamics unchanged. This leads to the ϕ\phi-MDP, a reward-redistributed counterpart of the original MDP.

Definition 3.4 (ϕ\phi-MDP).

Given an MDP-SCM ℳ\mathcal{M} and baseline policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}, the ϕ\phi-MDP ℳπϕ\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{\pi} replaces the reward function rr with the policy-induced Shapley reward:

rπϕ(s,x)=𝔼τ∼π[ϕt∣St=s,Xt=x],\displaystyle r^{\phi}_{\pi}(s,x)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi}[\phi_{t}\mid S_{t}=s,X_{t}=x], (8)

where the expectation is over trajectories τ\tau sampled from π\pi, conditioned on visiting (St,Xt)=(s,x)(S_{t},X_{t})=(s,x).

Lemma 3.5 (Gradient Equivalence).

For any baseline policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}}: 𝔼π​[∑tϕt⋅∇log⁡π​(Xt∣St)]=𝔼π​[Y⋅∑t∇log⁡π​(Xt∣St)]\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t}\phi_{t}\cdot\nabla\log\pi(X_{t}\mid S_{t})]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[Y\cdot\sum_{t}\nabla\log\pi(X_{t}\mid S_{t})].

Remark 3.6 (Independence under self-baseline).

The proof uses Y′⟂Xt|StY^{\prime}\perp X_{t}\mid S_{t} where Y′=Yσ𝟏Y^{\prime}=Y_{\sigma_{\mathbf{1}}} is the full-baseline outcome. Under self-baseline, Y′Y^{\prime} is computed on a counterfactual trajectory using fresh action samples X1:T′∼π(⋅∣S1:T𝟏)X^{\prime}_{1:T}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid S^{\mathbf{1}}_{1:T}), where S𝟏1:TS^{\mathbf{1}}_{1:T} denotes the counterfactual state sequence. Crucially, Y′Y^{\prime} carries no information about which specific action XtX_{t} was taken at the observed state StS_{t}: the counterfactual uses fresh action samples independent of XtX_{t}. The score function identity 𝔼Xt∼π​[∇log⁡π​(Xt∣St)]=0\mathbb{E}_{X_{t}\sim\pi}[\nabla\log\pi(X_{t}\mid S_{t})]=0 then gives 𝔼[Y′∇logπt]=0\mathbb{E}[Y^{\prime}\nabla\log\pi_{t}]=0.

Gradient equivalence means policy gradient algorithms receive the same update direction in expectation whether maximizing returns from MDP ℳ\mathcal{M} or its dual ϕ\phi-MDP.

Theorem 3.7 (Optimal Policy Equivalence).

ϕ\phi-MDP preserves optimal policies as the original MDP.

More specifically, arg⁡maxθ​𝔼πθ​[∑tϕt]=arg⁡maxθ​𝔼πθ​[Y]\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[\sum_{t}\phi_{t}]=\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}}[Y], so ϕ\phi-MDP is a drop-in replacement: any policy gradient algorithm applied to the redistributed rewards converges to the same optimal policy. One caveat: the ϕ\phi-MDP is undiscounted (γϕ=1\gamma_{\phi}=1). Since the NTE game outcome Y=∑tγt−1​rtY=\sum_{t}\gamma^{t-1}r_{t} already incorporates temporal discounting, applying γ\gamma to ϕt\phi_{t} would double-discount. The undiscounted ϕ\phi-return ∑tϕt\sum_{t}\phi_{t} equals Y−Y𝟏Y-Y^{\mathbf{1}} by Shapley efficiency.

3.3 How Causal Credit Assignment Helps Learning

We have shown that the ϕ\phi-MDP provides a principled credit assignment while preserving the optimal policy, but does it also improve learning efficiency? As an overview, Fig. 4 illustrates each mechanism visually. Below, we present the formal conditions our method helps policy optimization under the assumption of a finite second moment.

Assumption 3.8 (Finite Second Moment).

∀t,𝔼⁡[Yt2]≤σ2\forall t,\mathbb{E}[Y_{t}^{2}]\leq\sigma^{2}.

Proposition 3.9 (Sparse Causality).

Let k′=|{t:ϕt≠0}|k^{\prime}=|\{t:\phi_{t}\neq 0\}|, σϕ2=maxtVar[ϕt∇logπt]\sigma^{2}_{\phi}=\max_{t}\mathrm{Var}[\phi_{t}\nabla\!\log\pi_{t}], and ρ¯∈[0,1]\bar{\rho}\in[0,1] the maximal pairwise correlation among causal terms. Then Var⁡[g^ϕ]≤k′​(1+(k′−1)​ρ¯)​σϕ2\mathrm{Var}[\hat{g}^{\phi}]\leq k^{\prime}(1+(k^{\prime}{-}1)\bar{\rho})\,\sigma^{2}_{\phi}.

When few actions influence the outcome (k′≪Tk^{\prime}\ll T), ϕ\phi-values assign zero credit to non-causal actions, so only k′k^{\prime} terms contribute to gradient variance. The cross-correlation ρ¯\bar{\rho} is small in practice: the score function identity 𝔼⁡[∇log⁡πs∣Ss]=0\mathbb{E}[\nabla\!\log\pi_{s}\mid S_{s}]=0 decorrelates terms at distinct timesteps, and ρ¯=0\bar{\rho}=0 exactly in deterministic environments (Appendix C).

Proposition 3.10 (High Stochasticity).

Let 𝐳′=𝐳\mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\mathbf{z} with zt=1z_{t}=1 and ρY=Corr⁡[Y𝐳′,Y𝐳]\rho_{Y}=\mathrm{Corr}[Y^{\mathbf{z}^{\prime}},Y^{\mathbf{z}}] under shared exogenous randomness. Then Var⁡[ϕt]∝(1−ρY)\mathrm{Var}[\phi_{t}]\propto(1-\rho_{Y}).

Proposition 3.10 holds in expectation over coalitions 𝐳∼Q∗\mathbf{z}\sim Q^{*} and trajectories. Define the effective coupling ρ¯Y=𝔼𝐳∼Q∗​[Corr⁡[Y𝐳′,Y𝐳]]\bar{\rho}_{Y}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}\sim Q^{*}}[\mathrm{Corr}[Y^{\mathbf{z}^{\prime}},Y^{\mathbf{z}}]], averaging over the optimal coalition distribution. When a counterfactual trajectory diverges (off-track), fresh noise is sampled, reducing Corr⁡[Y𝐳′,Y𝐳]\mathrm{Corr}[Y^{\mathbf{z}^{\prime}},Y^{\mathbf{z}}] for that sample. The effective coupling ρ¯Y\bar{\rho}_{Y} is high when: (1) coalitions are small; (2) transitions are nearly deterministic; or (3) rewards depend on shared exogenous factors (unobserved confounders). Variance reduction is proportional to (1−ρ¯Y)(1-\bar{\rho}_{Y}).

Proposition 3.11 (Direct Propagation).

Tabular TD(0) with terminal-only reward requires O⁡(T)O(T) episodes for credit to reach the initial state. ϕ\phi-redistribution provides credit in O⁡(1)O(1) episodes via O⁡(T​Mδ,ϵ)O(TM_{\delta,\epsilon}) counterfactual simulations.

Remark 3.12 (Propagation Complexity).

For terminal-only reward: TD(0) requires O⁡(T)O(T) episodes and O⁡(T2)O(T^{2}) updates; ϕ\phi-redistribution requires O⁡(1)O(1) episodes and O⁡(T​Mδ,ϵ)O(TM_{\delta,\epsilon}) counterfactual simulations.

This shows that ϕ\phi-values avoid the delayed-effect and inefficient propagation problem of TD(0) methods. Though n-step returns, TD(λ\lambda) and the use of replay buffers mitigate this problem (Daley, 2025, Sec. 1.2-1.3), their core credit assumption rests on temporal proximity (Pignatelli et al., 2024). As the trajectory rolls out, reward in a distant step is deemed to be exponentially less likely caused by a given action (by the discounting factor). This clearly does not reflect an action’s true causal contribution as we have demonstrated in Fig. 1. And we will also see in experiment Sec. 5 that even with all the modern DRL techniques (Schulman et al., 2017; Schaul et al., 2016), existing algorithms still cannot solve those seemingly naive tabular MDPs due to the implicit time proximity assumption in credit assignment. And the most important implication of Prop. 3.11 is that our proposed ϕ\phi-value can allocate credit in a lossless and faithful way w.r.t each action’s actual causal contribution.

To sum, the “sweet spot” occurs when all three dimensions favor ϕ\phi-values: sparse causality (k′≪Tk^{\prime}\ll T), high stochasticity (ρY≈1\rho_{Y}\approx 1), and delayed reward. When both sparsity and stochasticity benefits apply, the variance reduction factors multiply: sparsity reduces contributing terms from TT to k′k^{\prime}, while coupled comparison reduces each term’s variance by (1−ρY)(1-\rho_{Y}), giving combined ratio k′T​(1−ρY)\frac{k^{\prime}}{T}(1-\rho_{Y}). On the other hand, there are cases when ϕ\phi-methods offer marginal advantage in terms of learning efficiency other than explanatory benefits over the standard TD methods when: (1) rewards are dense (k′≈Tk^{\prime}\approx T); (2) environment is deterministic (ρY\rho_{Y} is high); or (3) actions are rewarded immediately.

4 Estimating Counterfactual credit for Policy Optimization

This section develops efficient estimators for counterfactual Shapley values with O⁡(T​Mδ,ϵ)O(TM_{\delta,\epsilon}) total complexity, where Mδ,ϵ=σ2/((1−γ)2​δ​ϵ2)M_{\delta,\epsilon}=\sigma^{2}/((1-\gamma)^{2}\delta\epsilon^{2}), and integrates them into policy optimization as ϕ\phi-PPO.

Importance Sampling Equivalence.

Each coalition evaluation f⁡(𝐳)f(\mathbf{z}) requires O⁡(T)O(T) simulation time (Algo. 2). Computing TT Shapley values independently would require MM samples per value, yielding O⁡(T2​M)O(T^{2}M) total cost. The kernel formulation (Eq. 5) amortizes this: a single coalition evaluation updates all TT values via different kernel weights κt​(𝐳)\kappa_{t}(\mathbf{z}), reducing cost to O⁡(T​M)O(TM).

Definition 4.1 (Coalition Estimator).

Given samples 𝐳(m)∼Q\mathbf{z}^{(m)}\sim Q and NTE f⁡(𝐳)=Y−Y𝐳f(\mathbf{z})=Y-Y^{\mathbf{z}}, where Y𝐳≡Yσ𝐳Y^{\mathbf{z}}\equiv Y_{\sigma_{\mathbf{z}}} is the counterfactual return, the coalition estimator is ϕ^t=1M​∑m=1Mκt​(𝐳(m))Q⁡(𝐳(m))⋅f⁡(𝐳(m)).\hat{\phi}_{t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{\kappa_{t}(\mathbf{z}^{(m)})}{Q(\mathbf{z}^{(m)})}\cdot f(\mathbf{z}^{(m)}).

Under a mild assumption, we can derive the variance-reduction optimal proposal distribution Q∗​(𝐳)Q^{*}(\mathbf{z}) for coalition sampling.

Theorem 4.2 (Optimal Proposal).

Under Assumption 3.8, the variance-minimizing proposal is Q∗​(𝐳)=qk∗/(Tk)Q^{*}(\mathbf{z})=q^{*}_{k}/\binom{T}{k} where k=|𝐳|k=|\mathbf{z}| and qk∗∝ckq^{*}_{k}\propto\sqrt{c_{k}} with:

ck={1T​(1k+1T−k)k∈{1,…,T−1}1T2k=T\displaystyle c_{k}=\begin{cases}\frac{1}{T}\bigl(\frac{1}{k}+\frac{1}{T-k}\bigr)&k\in\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\\[4.0pt] \frac{1}{T^{2}}&k=T\end{cases} (9)

Under Q∗Q^{*}, the estimator achieves (ϵ,δ)(\epsilon,\delta)-accuracy with M=O⁡(Mδ,ϵ)M=O(M_{\delta,\epsilon}) samples.

The optimal qk∗∝ckq^{*}_{k}\propto\sqrt{c_{k}} concentrates on extreme coalition sizes (k≈1k\approx 1 or k≈T−1k\approx T-1) where kernel weights |κt||\kappa_{t}| are largest. In contrast to uniform sampling, which induces variance exponential in TT (extreme sizes have probability O⁡(2−T)O(2^{-T})), the optimal proposal achieves O⁡(1)O(1) second moment. Variance is low because YY and Y𝐳Y^{\mathbf{z}} share exogenous noise via common random numbers (Glasserman and Yao, 1992): the difference f⁡(𝐳)=Y−Y𝐳f(\mathbf{z})=Y-Y^{\mathbf{z}} isolates the effect of action choices while canceling environmental stochasticity. In practice, we also use antithetic sampling (Covert and Lee, 2021): each coalition 𝐳\mathbf{z} is paired with its complement 𝟏−𝐳\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{z} to further reduce variance.

Bootstrapped Estimation.

The basic estimator Def. (4.1) requires full trajectory simulation for each coalition. Bootstrapping with a learned value function V≈VπV\approx V_{\pi} reduces variance by replacing future counterfactual rewards with value estimates. We use TD-λ\lambda (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Sec. 12.2) that interpolates between Monte Carlo and bootstrapped estimates:

Gt𝐳,λ=yt𝐳+γ⁡[(1−λ)​V​(st+1𝐳)+λ​Gt+1𝐳,λ],\displaystyle G^{\mathbf{z},\lambda}_{t}=y^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}+\gamma[(1-\lambda)V(s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t+1})+\lambda G^{\mathbf{z},\lambda}_{t+1}], (10)

where λ=1\lambda=1 yields pure Monte Carlo (Gt𝐳,1=Yt𝐳G^{\mathbf{z},1}_{t}=Y^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}) and λ=0\lambda=0 yields one-step TD (Gt𝐳,0=yt𝐳+γ​V​(st+1𝐳)G^{\mathbf{z},0}_{t}=y^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}+\gamma V(s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t+1})). Then we define λ\lambda-bootstrapped NTE to decompose Y𝐳Y^{\mathbf{z}} into exact rewards before step tt and λ\lambda-returns from tt onwards. Let Rt𝐳=∑s<tγs−1​ys𝐳R^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=\sum_{s<t}\gamma^{s-1}y^{\mathbf{z}}_{s} denote the cumulative counterfactual reward before step tt. The per-step treatment effect is

ft𝐳=Y−(Rt𝐳+γt−1​Gt𝐳,λ).\displaystyle f^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=Y-(R^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}+\gamma^{t-1}G^{\mathbf{z},\lambda}_{t}). (11)

When λ=1\lambda=1, we have Rt𝐳+γt−1​Gt𝐳,1=Y𝐳R^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}+\gamma^{t-1}G^{\mathbf{z},1}_{t}=Y^{\mathbf{z}}, so ft𝐳=f⁡(𝐳)f^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}=f(\mathbf{z}) recovers the exact NTE. For λ<1\lambda<1, the identity 𝔼⁡[Gt𝐳,λ∣st𝐳]=Vπ​(st𝐳)+O⁡(ϵV)\mathbb{E}[G^{\mathbf{z},\lambda}_{t}\mid s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}]=V_{\pi}(s^{\mathbf{z}}_{t})+O(\epsilon_{V}) implies 𝔼⁡[ft𝐳]=f⁡(𝐳)+O⁡(ϵV)\mathbb{E}[f^{\mathbf{z}}_{t}]=f(\mathbf{z})+O(\epsilon_{V}) where ϵV=‖V−Vπ‖∞\epsilon_{V}=\|V-V_{\pi}\|_{\infty}.

Definition 4.3 (λ\lambda-Bootstrapped Estimator).

Given the per-step treatment effect ft𝐳f^{\mathbf{z}}_{t} Eq. (11), the λ\lambda-bootstrapped estimator is ϕ^tλ=1M​∑m=1Mκt​(𝐳(m))Q∗​(𝐳(m))⋅ft𝐳(m).\hat{\phi}^{\lambda}_{t}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{\kappa_{t}(\mathbf{z}^{(m)})}{Q^{*}(\mathbf{z}^{(m)})}\cdot f^{\mathbf{z}^{(m)}}_{t}.

By incorporating the contraction rate of λ\lambda-return (Tsitsiklis and Van Roy, 1997), we derive the following bias bound for our ϕ\phi-value estimator.

Theorem 4.4 (Bias Bound for ϕ^λ\hat{\phi}^{\lambda}).

Under Assumptions 3.3, 3.8: |𝔼⁡[ϕ^tλ]−ϕt|≤2​γ​(1−λ)1−γ​λ​‖V−Vπ‖∞.|\mathbb{E}[\hat{\phi}^{\lambda}_{t}]-\phi_{t}|\leq\frac{2\gamma(1-\lambda)}{1-\gamma\lambda}\|V-V_{\pi}\|_{\infty}.

The estimator is unbiased when λ=1\lambda=1 (pure MC) or ϵV=0\epsilon_{V}=0 (perfect value function). Decreasing λ\lambda trades bias for variance by truncating the effective horizon (Sutton and Barto, 2018, Ch. 12). Algo. 1 summarizes the overall procedure for counterfactual Shapley estimation.

ϕ\phi-PPO.

ϕ\phi-PPO integrates Shapley credit assignment into PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) via two mechanisms. First, the ϕ\phi-MDP ℳπϕ\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{\pi} (Definition 3.4) reformulates credit as per-step reward rπϕ(s,x)=𝔼[ϕt∣St=s,Xt=x]r^{\phi}_{\pi}(s,x)=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{t}\mid S_{t}=s,X_{t}=x], enabling standard actor-critic methods. Second, Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR) focuses updates on high-|ϕ||\phi| subtrajectories rather than individual transitions as in PER (Schaul et al., 2016). See Algo. 3 and Sec. B in appendix for the details. In each iteration, ϕ\phi-PPO samples sub-trajectories via PTR, computes ϕ\phi-estimates, and updates both values and policy networks. Advantages are normalized by batch standard deviation (not z-scored, to preserve ϕ=0\phi=0 as the no-effect baseline).

We admit that Algo. 1 requires O⁡(T​M)O(TM) value network evaluations per trajectory (one per counterfactual state per coalition sample) while standard PPO requires O⁡(T)O(T) evaluations. But this overhead is acceptable when: (1) value inference is cheaper than environment simulation for complex environments; (2) the MM evaluations can be batched for GPU efficiency. In practice, we use M=1M=1 coalition sample per trajectory, matching standard actor-critic overhead while still benefiting from counterfactual variance reduction.

5 Experiments

We evaluate ϕ\phi-PPO on two training benchmarks: SkillLuck (Sec. 5.1) and Combinatorial Lock (Sec. 5.2), illustrate ϕ\phi-value attributions on DoorKey (Sec. 5.3), and provide a controlled ablation on the Fork MDP in Appendix E.1. Throughout, a run succeeds iff P⁡(optimal)>0.9P(\text{optimal})>0.9 at all causal states for 200200 consecutive episodes. We compare all methods on total environment steps: ϕ\phi-PPO uses (1+M)​T(1{+}M)T steps per episode (11 observed trajectory plus MM counterfactual rollouts); all baselines use TT steps per episode. No method receives extra simulator access (full hyperparameters in Table 3). We compare against PPO, REINFORCE, and eight prior credit assignment methods: HCA-state, HCA-return (Harutyunyan et al., 2019b), CCA (Mesnard et al., 2021), CoCoA (Meulemans et al., 2023), QCA (Mesnard et al., 2023), RUDDER (Arjona-Medina et al., 2019), Synthetic Returns (Raposo et al., 2021), and H-DICE (Velu et al., 2024).

  1. Q1:

    Do ϕ\phi-values assign credit accurately, and does this translate into a learning advantage?

  2. Q2:

    Can ϕ\phi-PPO learn the optimal policy under delayed, sparse, and highly stochastic rewards?

  3. Q3:

    How sample efficient is ϕ\phi-PPO compared to vanilla PPO and prior credit assignment methods?

5.1 Skill vs. Luck

The SkillLuck MDP separates skill-based from luck-based rewards to test whether correct causal attributions translate into learning (Q1, Q2, Q3). The agent chooses from 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\} at each of T=100T{=}100 steps (γ=0.999\gamma{=}0.999, M=1M{=}1). Every reward includes i.i.d. noise 𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}); we sweep σ∈{0,3}\sigma\in\{0,3\} to test robustness to stochasticity. The first action x1x_{1} selects one of two branches. Actions at intermediate steps (2≤t≤T−22\leq t\leq T{-}2) do not affect the trajectory or reward. On the skill branch, the final action determines the reward: xT−1=1x_{T-1}{=}1 yields reward 11, while xT−1=0x_{T-1}{=}0 yields 00. On the luck branch, the agent receives a reward of Bern⁡(0.5)⋅γT−3\operatorname{Bern}(0.5)\cdot\gamma^{T-3} at step 22, regardless of any action. The γT−3\gamma^{T-3} scaling ensures both branches yield returns of comparable magnitude. Under the optimal final action, the skill branch has expected discounted return γT−2\gamma^{T-2} while the luck branch has 0.5​γT−20.5\gamma^{T-2}, so the optimal policy chooses skill. On the skill branch, two actions are causal: x1x_{1} and xT−1x_{T-1}. On the luck branch, only x1x_{1} is causal because it determines the branch; all subsequent actions have zero causal effect.

Predictions.

ϕ\phi-values should assign zero credit to xT−1x_{T-1} on luck (D1) and more credit to x1x_{1} on skill than luck (D4); Figure 1 confirms this. HCA fails because skill and luck branches share the same terminal observation. At T=100T{=}100, methods that cannot propagate delayed credit default to the luck branch.

Results (Figure 5).

At σ=0\sigma{=}0, several baselines match or exceed ϕ\phi-PPO because the noiseless setting poses no variance challenge; ϕ\phi-PPO’s slight shortfall reflects M=1M{=}1 approximation noise. HCA fails as predicted. At σ=3\sigma{=}3, the ranking reverses: ϕ\phi-PPO outperforms all baselines because shared noise cancels in the counterfactual difference (Proposition 3.10), while all other methods degrade. REINFORCE and PPO both fail, consistent with predictions. Among successful runs (right panel), ϕ\phi-PPO also converges fastest.

5.2 Combinatorial Lock

The Combinatorial Lock is a TT-step chain with tempting immediate rewards that tests delayed credit assignment (Q2, Q3). The agent chooses from 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\} at each position p∈{0,…,T−1}p\in\{0,\ldots,T{-}1\}: action 00 (Correct) advances to p+1p{+}1 with zero immediate reward; action 11 (Shortcut) terminates with immediate reward γT−p/2\gamma^{T-p}/2. Reaching position TT via TT consecutive Correct actions yields reward +1+1 (discounted return γT−1\gamma^{T-1}). The ratio of shortcut to optimal return is γ/2<1\gamma/2<1 at every position, so the shortcut is always suboptimal despite positive immediate reward. We sweep T∈{5,10,15,20,25}T\in\{5,10,15,20,25\} with γ=0.99\gamma=0.99 and M=16M{=}16 coalition samples. Every run begins with one optimal trajectory in the replay buffer so that all methods start from the same initial information. This isolates exploitation (can the method propagate credit from a known success?) from exploration, which becomes vanishingly unlikely as TT grows.

Predictions.

Every action along the optimal path is causal (k′/T=1k^{\prime}/T=1), so the sparse causality benefit (Proposition 3.9) does not apply. Combinatorial Lock isolates the delayed reward benefit (Proposition 3.11): (1) ϕ\phi-PPO should propagate credit from the terminal reward to position 00 in O⁡(1)O(1) episodes by evaluating full counterfactual returns; (2) TD-based methods require O⁡(T)O(T) bootstrap steps, and the shortcut temptation should lock the policy before credit reaches position 00, causing baseline success to collapse as TT grows.

Results (Figure 6).

Both predictions are confirmed. In the left panel, ϕ\phi-PPO + PTR (solid blue) is the only method that scales beyond T=10T{=}10; every baseline (dashed) collapses by T=15T{=}15. The right panel confirms that ϕ\phi-PPO + PTR converges at a roughly constant episode count across chain lengths, consistent with O⁡(1)O(1) propagation, while baselines flatline at the budget ceiling. Without PTR (solid orange), the seed trajectory is diluted by failures; PPO + PTR/PER (dashed) also fail, confirming that neither prioritized replay nor ϕ\phi-values alone suffice—both are necessary. Performance degrades at large TT because random coalition swaps are exponentially unlikely to preserve the full optimal path, so most counterfactual rollouts return zero and estimator variance increases.

5.3 DoorKey

We compute ϕ\phi-value attributions along an optimal trajectory in the 5×55{\times}5 DoorKey environment from MiniGrid (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2018) (Q1). The agent selects from 7 actions (navigation, pickup, toggle, etc.) across |𝒮|=400|\mathcal{S}|=400 states (5×55{\times}5 grid ×\times 4 orientations ×\times 2 key states ×\times 2 door states). The optimal trajectory reaches the goal in 13 steps.

Baseline choice determines the causal story.

Under a uniform random baseline (top right), ϕt\phi_{t} is nearly uniform because DoorKey is a serial dependency chain in which every step must be correct for success. Values taper after the door toggle (t=8t{=}8) because a random agent increasingly reaches the goal by chance from nearby states. Under a navigation-only baseline (bottom right), the causal story changes entirely. The navigator already takes the correct action at post-door states, so those actions receive ϕt≈0\phi_{t}\approx 0 (D1, causal admissibility). Pickup, toggle, and first-room navigation steps that the navigator cannot replicate receive nonzero ϕt\phi_{t} (D2, causal power), splitting the total credit equally. ϕ\phi-values thus measure credit relative to the baseline policy, not in absolute terms. Notably, the key pickup (t=3t{=}3) receives comparable ϕt\phi_{t} to the door toggle (t=8t{=}8) under both baselines, despite zero immediate reward; its value reflects the downstream effect of enabling the toggle five steps later, confirming that ϕ\phi-values propagate credit through dependent subgoal chains (Proposition 3.11).

Across all benchmarks, ϕ\phi-PPO converges in fewer episodes than every baseline. At M=1M{=}1 (SkillLuck), the 2×2{\times} per-episode cost is offset by ≥4×{\geq}4{\times} fewer episodes; at M=16M{=}16 (Lock), ϕ\phi-PPO wins on episode efficiency but not total simulation budget, motivating future variance reduction work.

6 Conclusion

We introduced Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment, a principled framework that addresses the fundamental temporal credit assignment problem by grounding reward attribution in causal theory via Structural Causal Models. By utilizing the Counterfactual Shapley Value (ϕ\phi-value), we isolate an agent’s true causal contribution from environmental stochasticity and spurious correlations, inducing a dual ϕ\phi-MDP that preserves the original optimal policy while providing significantly clearer learning signals. Our framework specifically addresses the challenges of high stochasticity, sparse causality, and delayed rewards through a computationally efficient linear-time estimator and the resulting ϕ\phi-PPO algorithm. Empirical results across challenging benchmarks demonstrate that ϕ\phi-PPO achieves superior sample efficiency and convergence compared to existing baselines, offering a scalable and theoretically sound path toward more efficient and explainable reinforcement learning.

Appendix A Counterfactual Simulation

Appendix B ϕ\phi-PPO

ϕ\phi-PPO integrates Shapley credit assignment into PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) via two mechanisms. First, the ϕ\phi-MDP ℳπϕ\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{\pi} (Definition 3.4) reformulates credit as per-step reward rπϕ(s,x)=𝔼[ϕt∣St=s,Xt=x]r^{\phi}_{\pi}(s,x)=\mathbb{E}[\phi_{t}\mid S_{t}=s,X_{t}=x], enabling standard actor-critic methods. Second, Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR) focuses policy updates on high-|ϕ||\phi| actions when credit is sparse.

Intuition.

Compared to standard PPO, ϕ\phi-PPO makes three changes: (1) replace per-step rewards rtr_{t} with Shapley values ϕ^t\hat{\phi}_{t}, which isolate causal contribution from return noise; (2) add a second value network VψV_{\psi} for bootstrapping counterfactual simulations (Algo. 1); the standard PPO value network VωϕV^{\phi}_{\omega} remains, now estimating advantages on the ϕ\phi-MDP; (3) use PTR to select trajectories for replay. Compared to standard PER (Schaul et al., 2015b), PTR prioritizes by |ϕt||\phi_{t}| (causal impact) rather than TD error |δt||\delta_{t}|. Consider Pong: when the ball moves away from the paddle, actions have no causal effect on the outcome, yet TD error may be high if the value network is inaccurate. TD-error PER would wastefully prioritize these non-causal states; PTR correctly assigns low priority since |ϕt|≈0|\phi_{t}|\approx 0. Conversely, if the policy network learns slower than the value network, TD error is low but the policy remains suboptimal at causally important states. PTR correctly prioritizes these states because |ϕt||\phi_{t}| reflects whether the action matters, not whether the value estimate is accurate.

Realized estimates ϕ^t\hat{\phi}_{t} yield unbiased policy gradients when substituted for rπϕr^{\phi}_{\pi}. By Theorem 4.4 with λ=1\lambda=1, 𝔼⁡[ϕ^t∣τ]=ϕt\mathbb{E}[\hat{\phi}_{t}\mid\tau]=\phi_{t}, where τ=(s1:T,x1:T,y1:T)\tau=(s_{1:T},x_{1:T},y_{1:T}) denotes the trajectory. The law of iterated expectations then gives 𝔼[ϕ^t∣st,xt]=rπϕ(st,xt)\mathbb{E}[\hat{\phi}_{t}\mid s_{t},x_{t}]=r^{\phi}_{\pi}(s_{t},x_{t}).

The algorithm maintains two value networks: Vψ≈VπV_{\psi}\approx V_{\pi} for bootstrapping counterfactual simulations in Algo. 1, and Vωϕ≈VπϕV^{\phi}_{\omega}\approx V^{\phi}_{\pi} for computing ϕ\phi-advantages.

ϕ\phi-Advantages.

Let ϕ^t\hat{\phi}_{t} denote the Shapley estimate from Algo. 1. The ϕ\phi-TD error measures one-step prediction error using ϕ^t\hat{\phi}_{t} as reward:

δtϕ=ϕ^t+Vωϕ​(st+1)−Vωϕ​(st).\displaystyle\delta_{t}^{\phi}=\hat{\phi}_{t}+V^{\phi}_{\omega}(s_{t+1})-V^{\phi}_{\omega}(s_{t}). (12)

The ϕ\phi-advantage generalizes GAE (Schulman et al., 2015) to the ϕ\phi-MDP:

Atϕ=∑ℓ=0T−t(λϕ)ℓ​δt+ℓϕ,\displaystyle A_{t}^{\phi}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T-t}(\lambda^{\phi})^{\ell}\delta_{t+\ell}^{\phi}, (13)

where λϕ∈[0,1]\lambda^{\phi}\in[0,1] controls the bias-variance tradeoff (distinct from λ\lambda in Algo. 1, which controls bootstrapping depth). The ϕ\phi-return is

Gtϕ=∑ℓ=0T−tϕ^t+ℓ,\displaystyle G_{t}^{\phi}=\sum_{\ell=0}^{T-t}\hat{\phi}_{t+\ell}, (14)

which serves as the training target for VωϕV^{\phi}_{\omega} (Eq. 22). Shapley efficiency ensures ∑tϕt=Y−Y∅\sum_{t}\phi_{t}=Y-Y_{\emptyset}, where Y∅Y_{\emptyset} is the baseline return (all-default actions); the sum of per-step credit equals the total reward improvement.

Adaptive fresh/replay ratio.

Each training iteration mixes fresh rollouts with replay from the priority buffer. A static fresh probability ξ\xi is suboptimal: early in training, fresh rollouts discover high-|ϕ||\phi| states; later, replay exploits known high-impact actions. We adapt ξ\xi via Thompson sampling (Russo et al., 2018).

Let pj=maxt⁡pj,tp_{j}=\max_{t}p_{j,t} denote the trajectory-level priority, where pj,tp_{j,t} is the priority from Eq. (20) below. A fresh trajectory “wins” if pj>p¯ℬp_{j}>\bar{p}_{\mathcal{B}}. Here p¯ℬ=∑i∈ℬpi2/∑i∈ℬpi\bar{p}_{\mathcal{B}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}p_{i}^{2}/\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}p_{i} is the expected priority under proportional sampling. Let u∈[0,1]u\in[0,1] denote the fraction of fresh trajectories that win. We track (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), initialized to (1,1)(1,1), via exponential moving averages with decay γξ<1\gamma_{\xi}<1:

α←γξ​α+u,β←γξ​β+(1−u).\displaystyle\alpha\leftarrow\gamma_{\xi}\alpha+u,\quad\beta\leftarrow\gamma_{\xi}\beta+(1-u). (15)

The decay discounts old observations to adapt to non-stationarity. At steady state α+β→1/(1−γξ)\alpha+\beta\to 1/(1-\gamma_{\xi}), bounding the effective sample size.

At each iteration, sample ξ∼Beta⁡(α+1,β+1)\xi\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha+1,\beta+1) and collect nfresh=clamp⁡(⌊ξ​B⌋,1,B−1)n_{\mathrm{fresh}}=\mathrm{clamp}(\lfloor\xi B\rfloor,1,B{-}1) fresh rollouts. Stratified sampling reduces variance in the fresh/replay ratio compared to per-trajectory Bernoulli sampling.

Importance-sampling corrections.

The IS correction depends on the trajectory source. Both fresh and replay trajectories use the PPO ratio for multi-epoch updates:

rj,t=πθ​(xj,t∣sj,t)/πθold​(xj,t∣sj,t),\displaystyle r_{j,t}=\pi_{\theta}(x_{j,t}\mid s_{j,t})/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(x_{j,t}\mid s_{j,t}), (16)

where πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} is the policy snapshot at the start of the current training step. The clipped surrogate objective (Schulman et al., 2017) prevents large policy updates:

ℓ⁡(r,A)=−min⁡(r​A,clip⁡(r,1−ϵclip,1+ϵclip)​A).\displaystyle\ell(r,A)=-\min\bigl(rA,\;\mathrm{clip}(r,1{-}\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1{+}\epsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})A\bigr). (17)

Replay trajectories additionally require a PTR importance-sampling weight to correct for priority-based sampling. Let Pj=pj/∑i∈ℬpiP_{j}=p_{j}/\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}p_{i} denote the sampling probability for trajectory jj from buffer ℬ\mathcal{B}. The normalized IS weight is:

wj=(|ℬ|⋅Pj)−βis/maxj′∈ℬ⁡(|ℬ|⋅Pj′)−βis.\displaystyle w_{j}=(|\mathcal{B}|\cdot P_{j})^{-\beta_{\mathrm{is}}}\big/\max_{j^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}(|\mathcal{B}|\cdot P_{j^{\prime}})^{-\beta_{\mathrm{is}}}. (18)

The exponent βis\beta_{\mathrm{is}} anneals from 00 to 11 over training; at βis=1\beta_{\mathrm{is}}=1, the weights fully correct for non-uniform sampling. Since ϕ\phi-values are recomputed for replay trajectories using the current policy and value function, no policy importance weight is needed.

The full policy loss applies the PTR weight only to replay trajectories:

ℒθPTR=1B​∑j=1Bw~j​∑t=1Tℓ⁡(rj,t,Atϕ),w~j={1if ​j​ is freshwjif ​j​ is replay.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{PTR}}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{j=1}^{B}\tilde{w}_{j}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\ell(r_{j,t},A_{t}^{\phi}),\quad\tilde{w}_{j}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }j\text{ is fresh}\\ w_{j}&\text{if }j\text{ is replay}\end{cases}. (19)

PTR: Priority computation.

When credit is sparse, PTR focuses updates on high-impact actions. The priority for state sts_{t} is

pt=(ϕt(2))αptr/2+ϵptr,\displaystyle p_{t}=(\phi^{(2)}_{t})^{\alpha_{\mathrm{ptr}}/2}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{ptr}}, (20)

where ϕt(2)\phi^{(2)}_{t} is a bias-corrected exponential moving average (Kingma and Ba, 2015) of squared Shapley estimates. The priority ϕ(2)\sqrt{\phi^{(2)}} is an exponentially-weighted root-mean-square (RMS), capturing both mean magnitude and variance: 𝔼⁡[ϕ2]=μ2+σ2\sqrt{\mathbb{E}[\phi^{2}]}=\sqrt{\mu^{2}+\sigma^{2}}. This prioritizes states where (i) actions have consistent causal impact (high |μ||\mu|), and (ii) the action choice matters but the policy has not yet converged (high σ\sigma with μ≈0\mu\approx 0). The exponent αptr\alpha_{\mathrm{ptr}} controls priority sharpness; ϵptr\epsilon_{\mathrm{ptr}} prevents starvation.

Priority decay. Priorities become stale as the policy improves. Each iteration, all priorities decay by pj←γp​pjp_{j}\leftarrow\gamma_{p}p_{j}, where γp∈[0.99,0.9999]\gamma_{p}\in[0.99,0.9999]. Trajectories with pj<ϵevictp_{j}<\epsilon_{\mathrm{evict}} are evicted, implicitly bounding the buffer size to O⁡(log⁡(ϵevict)/log⁡(γp))O(\log(\epsilon_{\mathrm{evict}})/\log(\gamma_{p})) iterations of data.

Training.

Three components train jointly. The value network VψV_{\psi} for counterfactual bootstrapping trains on both actual and counterfactual TD errors from Algo. 1:

ℒV=1(M+1)​B​T​(∑j,tδj,t2+∑j,t,m(δj,t𝐳(m))2).\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{V}=\textstyle\frac{1}{(M{+}1)BT}\Bigl(\sum_{j,t}\delta_{j,t}^{2}+\sum_{j,t,m}(\delta^{\mathbf{z}^{(m)}}_{j,t})^{2}\Bigr). (21)

The ϕ\phi-critic VωϕV^{\phi}_{\omega} regresses to the ϕ\phi-return:

ℒVϕ=1B​T​∑j,t(Gj,tϕ−Vωϕ​(sj,t))2.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{V^{\phi}}=\textstyle\frac{1}{BT}\sum_{j,t}(G_{j,t}^{\phi}-V^{\phi}_{\omega}(s_{j,t}))^{2}. (22)

Following Schulman et al. (2017), all three components train via a single combined loss with gradient clipping (norm gmaxg_{\max}):

ℒ∗=ℒθPTR+c1​ℒV+c2​ℒVϕ−c3​H​(πθ),\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{*}=\mathcal{L}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{PTR}}+c_{1}\mathcal{L}_{V}+c_{2}\mathcal{L}_{V^{\phi}}-c_{3}H(\pi_{\theta}), (23)

where c1,c2c_{1},c_{2} weight the value losses and c3c_{3} weights the entropy bonus H⁡(πθ)=−𝔼s∼dπ​[∑xπθ​(x∣s)​log⁡πθ​(x∣s)]H(\pi_{\theta})=-\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d_{\pi}}\bigl[\sum_{x}\pi_{\theta}(x\mid s)\log\pi_{\theta}(x\mid s)\bigr] (Schulman et al., 2017) (Table 3).

Algorithm.

Algo. 3 summarizes ϕ\phi-PPO. Each iteration samples subtrajectories via PTR, computes ϕ\phi-estimates, and updates all three networks. Advantages are normalized by batch standard deviation (not z-scored, to preserve ϕ=0\phi=0 as the no-effect baseline).

Guarantees.

ϕ\phi-PPO inherits theoretical properties from its components.

Gradient equivalence. By Lemma 3.5, ϕ\phi-values produce the same expected policy gradient as original returns: 𝔼[∑tϕt∇logπt]=𝔼[Y∑t∇logπt]\mathbb{E}[\sum_{t}\phi_{t}\nabla\log\pi_{t}]=\mathbb{E}[Y\sum_{t}\nabla\log\pi_{t}]. Thus ϕ\phi-PPO targets the same optimum as standard PPO.

Bootstrap bias. The λ\lambda-return (Eq. 10) introduces bias bounded by O⁡(γ⁡(1−λ)​ϵV/(1−γ​λ))O(\gamma(1{-}\lambda)\epsilon_{V}/(1{-}\gamma\lambda)) where ϵV=‖V−Vπ‖∞\epsilon_{V}=\|V-V_{\pi}\|_{\infty} (Theorem 4.4). This bias vanishes as Vψ→VπV_{\psi}\to V_{\pi}.

Trajectory replay. Because ϕ\phi-values are defined over trajectories (Definition 3.4), PTR replays entire subtrajectories rather than individual transitions. This is sound by Corollary C.4: for any state ss and horizon nn, the optimal policy in the undiscounted truncated ϕ\phi-MDP ℳnϕ​(s)\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{n}(s) equals the optimal policy in ℳ\mathcal{M}. Since Vϕ,∗=0V^{\phi,*}=0 under self-baseline at optimality, no bootstrap is needed in the exact case; in practice, V^ϕ≈0\hat{V}^{\phi}\approx 0 during training. IS weights (Eq. 18) correct for the prioritized sampling distribution, ensuring unbiased gradient estimates.

Hyperparameters are in Table 3; proofs in Appendix D.4.

Appendix C Theory Details

Definition C.1 (Functional Dependence).

Given world (ℳ,𝐮)(\mathcal{M},\mathbf{u}), the functional dependence of YY on XX under baseline z=(x′,𝐳′)z=(x^{\prime},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}) is:

c⁡(ℳ,𝐮,X,Y,z)=Y𝐳′​(𝐮)−Y𝐳′,x′​(𝐮)\displaystyle c(\mathcal{M},\mathbf{u},X,Y,z)=Y_{\mathbf{z}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u})-Y_{\mathbf{z}^{\prime},x^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u}) (24)

The baseline space is 𝒵={(x′,𝐳′):x′∈𝒟X,𝐙⊆𝐗∖{X},𝐳′∈𝒟𝐙}\mathcal{Z}=\{(x^{\prime},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}):x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{X},\mathbf{Z}\subseteq\mathbf{X}\setminus\{X\},\mathbf{z}^{\prime}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathbf{Z}}\} equipped with probability measure Pℳ​(𝐙,X)P^{\mathcal{M}}(\mathbf{Z},X).

This measures the outcome difference when XX changes from baseline x′x^{\prime} to its actual value, with other variables held at 𝐳′\mathbf{z}^{\prime}. When 𝐳′=∅\mathbf{z}^{\prime}=\emptyset, this reduces to the unit-level total effect Y​(𝐮)−Yx′​(𝐮)Y(\mathbf{u})-Y_{x^{\prime}}(\mathbf{u}). Functional dependence captures the counterfactual test: if changing XX changes YY, then XX is responsible for YY. This condition is necessary for causation across major definitions in the actual causation literature (Halpern, 2016; Beckers and Vennekens, 2018; Beckers, 2021).

To formalize the condition, we introduce the why-query Why⁡(Y∣𝐞;𝐗)\mathrm{Why}(Y\mid\mathbf{e};\mathbf{X}), composed of three parts:

  1. (1)

    the event being explained, or explanandum, Y=yY=y, inducing alternate values, or foils, Y=y′≠yY=y^{\prime}\neq y;

  2. (2)

    the evidence 𝐄=𝐞\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{e}, the observed context used to infer causes; and

  3. (3)

    the explanatory variables 𝐗⊆𝐕\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}, which prescribe the subset of variables to attribute to.11 1 Explicitly selecting the set of explanatory variables as a subset of observed variables allows us to exclude irrelevant or unobserved causes such as “Alice arriving” or “the Big Bang”, even though it is true that if Alice did not arrive, or the Big Bang did not occur, the funding outcome would be different!

We write Why⁡(y∣𝐞)\mathrm{Why}(y\mid\mathbf{e}) as shorthand for Why⁡(Y=y∣𝐞;𝐗)\mathrm{Why}(Y{=}y\mid\mathbf{e};\mathbf{X}) when 𝐗\mathbf{X} is clear from context.

Given a why-query, an Explanatory Variable Attribution (EVA) assigns a numerical attribution to each explanatory variable in 𝐗\mathbf{X}.

Definition C.2 (Explanatory Variable Attribution).

An explanatory variable attribution (EVA) is a function ϕ:Ω×𝕎×𝐗→ℝ\phi:\Omega\times\mathbb{W}\times\mathbf{X}\to\mathbb{R}, where Ω\Omega is the space of SCMs over 𝐕\mathbf{V} and 𝕎\mathbb{W} is the space of why-queries Why⁡(Y∣𝐞;𝐗)\mathrm{Why}(Y\mid\mathbf{e};\mathbf{X}) asking why Y=y∈𝐞Y=y\in\mathbf{e}, given evidence 𝐄=𝐞\mathbf{E}=\mathbf{e}, in terms of variables 𝐗⊆𝐕∖{Y}\mathbf{X}\subseteq\mathbf{V}\setminus\{Y\}.

With EVA, we are ready to formally define the Causal Credit Assignment criteria from Def. 3.1.

Definition C.3 (Causal Credit Assignment, formal).

We define four desiderata as mappings D1:4:Ω×ℂ×Φ→{0,1}D_{1:4}:\Omega\times\mathbb{C}\times\Phi\to\{0,1\}, where ℂ\mathbb{C} is the space of causal measures and Φ\Phi is the space of EVAs. Given SCM ℳ∈Ω\mathcal{M}\in\Omega, causal measure c∈ℂc\in\mathbb{C}, and EVA ϕ∈Φ\phi\in\Phi, we say Di​(ℳ,c,ϕ)=1D_{i}(\mathcal{M},c,\phi)=1 when:

D1:\displaystyle D_{1}:\quad c=0⟹ϕ=𝟎\displaystyle c=0\implies\phi=\mathbf{0} (Causal Admissibility)
D2:\displaystyle D_{2}:\quad ∃𝐮,z:c≠0⟹ϕ≠𝟎\displaystyle\exists\mathbf{u},z:c\neq 0\implies\phi\neq\mathbf{0} (Causal Power)
D3:\displaystyle D_{3}:\quad cℳ=cℳ′∧Pc¯ℳ​(Z)≢Pc¯ℳ′​(Z)∧P+ℳ​(z)≥P+ℳ′​(z)\displaystyle c_{\mathcal{M}}=c_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}\land P^{\mathcal{M}}_{\bar{c}}(Z)\not\equiv P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{\bar{c}}(Z)\land P^{\mathcal{M}}_{+}(z)\geq P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{+}(z)
⟹ϕℳ>ϕℳ′\displaystyle\implies\phi_{\mathcal{M}}>\phi_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}} (Causal Normality)
D4:\displaystyle D_{4}:\quad cℳ≥cℳ′∧Pℳ​(Z)≡Pℳ′​(Z)∧Pℳ​(cZ)≢Pℳ′​(cZ)\displaystyle c_{\mathcal{M}}\geq c_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}\land P^{\mathcal{M}}(Z)\equiv P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}(Z)\land P^{\mathcal{M}}(c_{Z})\not\equiv P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}(c_{Z})
⟹ϕℳ>ϕℳ′\displaystyle\implies\phi_{\mathcal{M}}>\phi_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}} (Causal Effect Scaling)

Quantification: all premises universally quantified unless marked ∃\exists. Notation: cc, cℳc_{\mathcal{M}} abbreviate c⁡(ℳ,𝐮,X,Y,z)c(\mathcal{M},\mathbf{u},X,Y,z); ϕ\phi, ϕℳ\phi_{\mathcal{M}} abbreviate ϕX​(ℳ,w)\phi_{X}(\mathcal{M},w); P≡P′P\equiv P^{\prime} denotes distributional equality; Pc¯ℳ​(Z)≔Pℳ​(Z∣c≠0)P^{\mathcal{M}}_{\bar{c}}(Z)\coloneqq P^{\mathcal{M}}(Z\mid c\neq 0); P+ℳ​(z)≔sign⁡(cℳ)⋅Pℳ​(z)P^{\mathcal{M}}_{+}(z)\coloneqq\mathrm{sign}(c_{\mathcal{M}})\cdot P^{\mathcal{M}}(z).

Chunk-size Updates.

Theorem 3.7 establishes optimality equivalence for full-length trajectories optimization. In practice, we chunk trajectories: each chunk begins at an arbitrary state ss (sampled from a replay buffer) and extends for nn steps with a value bootstrap at the end. The following corollary shows that both modifications—arbitrary starting state and finite-horizon truncation—preserve the optimal policy.

Corollary C.4 (Chunked ϕ\phi-Learning).

For any state ss and horizon nn, let ℳnϕ​(s)\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{n}(s) denote the undiscounted ϕ\phi-MDP starting from ss with actions x1:nx_{1:n} and terminal value Vϕ​(sn)V^{\phi}(s_{n}). The optimal policy in ℳnϕ​(s)\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{n}(s) equals the optimal policy in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

The corollary holds for any state ss, not only the initial state distribution. This justifies experience replay: sampling (st,xt)(s_{t},x_{t}) from a buffer and computing ϕt:t+n\phi_{t:t+n} yields correct policy updates regardless of trajectory origin. Under self-baseline at optimality, Vϕ,∗​(s)=0V^{\phi,*}(s)=0 for all ss (Shapley efficiency), so no bootstrap is needed in the exact case. In practice, V^ϕ≈0\hat{V}^{\phi}\approx 0 during training, and the bootstrap error vanishes as the policy converges. This enables Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR) using |ϕt||\phi_{t}| as priority. TD-error prioritization samples states where the value function is inaccurate, but accurate values do not guarantee optimal actions. In contrast, |ϕt||\phi_{t}| measures causal contribution: large |ϕt||\phi_{t}| indicates the action significantly affected the outcome. Policy improvement at states with large |ϕt||\phi_{t}| affects returns the most. When credit is sparse (k′≪Tk^{\prime}\ll T causal actions), non-causal state-action pairs have ϕt≈0\phi_{t}\approx 0 and receive minimal priority, concentrating updates on the causally-relevant subset.

D3 (Causal Normality). Consider two SCMs ℳ,ℳ′\mathcal{M},\mathcal{M}^{\prime} with identical causal effects (cℳ=cℳ′c_{\mathcal{M}}=c_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}) but different baseline distributions satisfying P+ℳ​(z)≥P+ℳ′​(z)P^{\mathcal{M}}_{+}(z)\geq P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{+}(z). When P+ℳ​(z)≥P+ℳ′​(z)P^{\mathcal{M}}_{+}(z)\geq P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}_{+}(z), the baseline under ℳ\mathcal{M} assigns weakly higher probability to baselines that produce positive causal effects. Each marginal contribution f⁡(𝐳∪{t})−f⁡(𝐳)f(\mathbf{z}\cup\{t\})-f(\mathbf{z}) measures the additional effect of intervening at step tt. Under ℳ\mathcal{M}, the “default” behavior (baseline) is more aligned with positive outcomes, so the departure from baseline caused by XtX_{t} receives greater credit. Formally, the Shapley value is the expected marginal contribution over uniformly random orderings; since each marginal contribution under ℳ\mathcal{M} weakly exceeds that under ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} (by the monotonicity of the NTE in baseline probabilities when the causal effect sign is fixed), we obtain ϕℳ>ϕℳ′\phi_{\mathcal{M}}>\phi_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}.

D4 (Causal Effect Scaling). Consider two SCMs with identical baseline distributions (Pℳ​(Z)≡Pℳ′​(Z)P^{\mathcal{M}}(Z)\equiv P^{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}(Z)) but cℳ≥cℳ′c_{\mathcal{M}}\geq c_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}} (larger causal effect in ℳ\mathcal{M}). Since baseline distributions are identical, the Shapley weights are the same in both games. By the Shapley monotonicity property (if player tt’s marginal contribution in game vv weakly exceeds that in game v′v^{\prime} for every coalition, then ϕt​(v)≥ϕt​(v′)\phi_{t}(v)\geq\phi_{t}(v^{\prime})), we obtain ϕℳ>ϕℳ′\phi_{\mathcal{M}}>\phi_{\mathcal{M}^{\prime}}. ∎

The ϕ\phi-MDP ℳπϕ\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{\pi} has a well-defined value function Vϕ​(s)=𝔼⁡[∑ℓ≥0ϕt+ℓ∣St=s]V^{\phi}(s)=\mathbb{E}[\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\phi_{t+\ell}\mid S_{t}=s] satisfying the Bellman equation Vϕ(s)=𝔼x∼π[rπϕ(s,x)+𝔼s′∼P(⋅∣s,x)[Vϕ(s′)]]V^{\phi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\pi}[r^{\phi}_{\pi}(s,x)+\mathbb{E}_{s^{\prime}\sim P(\cdot\mid s,x)}[V^{\phi}(s^{\prime})]]. Proof.

The proof proceeds in two steps, corresponding to the two truncations.

Step 1: Arbitrary initial state.

Theorem 3.7 shows that the optimal policy in ℳϕ\mathcal{M}^{\phi} equals the optimal policy in ℳ\mathcal{M}. By the Markov property, the optimal policy π∗​(x∣s)\pi^{*}(x\mid s) depends only on the current state ss, not on the initial state distribution or the trajectory history. Therefore, π∗\pi^{*} is optimal in ℳϕ​(s)\mathcal{M}^{\phi}(s) for any starting state ss. This justifies experience replay: transitions sampled from a buffer correspond to different starting states, but all yield the same optimal policy.

Step 2: Finite horizon with value bootstrap.

Consider the nn-step truncated ϕ\phi-MDP ℳnϕ​(s)\mathcal{M}^{\phi}_{n}(s) with terminal value Vϕ​(sn)V^{\phi}(s_{n}). Since the ϕ\phi-MDP is undiscounted (γϕ=1\gamma_{\phi}=1, Corollary D.3), the objective is:

Jnϕ​(s)=𝔼π​[∑t=1nϕt+Vϕ​(sn)∣S1=s].\displaystyle J_{n}^{\phi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\phi_{t}+V^{\phi}(s_{n})\mid S_{1}=s\right]. (27)

Therefore Vϕ,∗​(s)=0V^{\phi,*}(s)=0 for all ss, and the nn-step objective simplifies to Jnϕ​(s)=𝔼π​[∑t=1nϕt∣S1=s]J_{n}^{\phi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\phi_{t}\mid S_{1}=s]. By Lemma 3.5 applied to the nn-step game (the proof uses Assumption 3.3 step-by-step and carries through for any finite horizon), ∇θ𝔼π​[∑t=1nϕt]=∇θ𝔼π​[∑t=1nγt−1​rt]\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\phi_{t}]=\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t=1}^{n}\gamma^{t-1}r_{t}]. The RHS is the gradient of the standard nn-step return, whose maximizer is π∗\pi^{*}. Since JnϕJ_{n}^{\phi} and the standard objective share the same gradient for all θ\theta, they have the same maximizer.

Approximate case.

In practice, VϕV^{\phi} is learned, not zero, so we bootstrap with V^ϕ​(sn)≈Vϕ,∗​(sn)=0\hat{V}^{\phi}(s_{n})\approx V^{\phi,*}(s_{n})=0. The bootstrap error |V^ϕ​(sn)||\hat{V}^{\phi}(s_{n})| introduces bias; as training converges (V^ϕ→0\hat{V}^{\phi}\to 0), the bias vanishes. This parallels the standard nn-step bias-variance tradeoff: shorter chunks reduce variance from trajectory noise at the cost of bootstrap bias. ∎

D.5 PTR Buffer Design (Section B)

PTR stores full trajectories with per-timestep priorities. The priority formula uses a smoothed estimate:

pt=(ϕt(2))αptr/2+ϵptr,\displaystyle p_{t}=(\phi^{(2)}_{t})^{\alpha_{\mathrm{ptr}}/2}+\epsilon_{\mathrm{ptr}}, (35)

where ϕt(2)\phi^{(2)}_{t} is a bias-corrected exponential moving average (Kingma and Ba, 2015) of squared Shapley estimates, αptr\alpha_{\mathrm{ptr}} controls priority sharpness, and ϵptr\epsilon_{\mathrm{ptr}} prevents starvation. Sampling selects (trajectory, starting timestep) pairs proportionally to ptp_{t} using the Gumbel-max trick for efficient vectorized sampling. When the buffer reaches capacity, the trajectory with lowest total priority ∑tpt\sum_{t}p_{t} is evicted.

Following standard PER (Schaul et al., 2015b), we apply importance sampling (IS) correction to account for the non-uniform sampling distribution. Let pip_{i} denote the priority of sample ii in the buffer. Each sampled subtrajectory receives weight wi=(|ℬ|⋅pi/∑jpj)−βisw_{i}=(|\mathcal{B}|\cdot p_{i}/\sum_{j}p_{j})^{-\beta_{\mathrm{is}}}, normalized by maxi⁡wi\max_{i}w_{i} for stability. The exponent βis\beta_{\mathrm{is}} anneals from β0\beta_{0} (e.g., 0.4) to 1 over training, providing full bias correction at convergence while allowing faster early learning.

Appendix E Additional Experiments

This section contains additional experiments validating the theoretical predictions.

E.1 Fork MDP

The Fork MDP isolates the three variance reduction benefits of ϕ\phi-PPO. The agent chooses from 𝒜={0,1}\mathcal{A}=\{0,1\} at each of TT steps (γ=0.99\gamma{=}0.99). Only the first cc actions affect the terminal reward: YT∼𝒩⁡(1,σ2)Y_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(1,\sigma^{2}) if x1=⋯=xc=0x_{1}=\cdots=x_{c}=0 (the optimal actions), YT∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)Y_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) otherwise. Intermediate rewards are i.i.d. noise Yt∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2)Y_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}) for t<Tt<T. The environment combines sparse causality (k′=c≪Tk^{\prime}=c\ll T, Proposition 3.9), high stochasticity (shared noise cancels in the counterfactual difference, Proposition 3.10), and delayed reward (YTY_{T} only, Proposition 3.11).

Results (Figure 8).

At the default configuration (T=100T{=}100, σ=10\sigma{=}10, c=1c{=}1), ϕ\phi-PPO achieves 100%100\% success, while REINFORCE degrades to ∼58%{\sim}58\% and PPO fails at ∼5%{\sim}5\%. Each column isolates one benefit: noise cancellation (a), horizon independence (b), and causal isolation (c). The bottom row confirms that ϕ\phi-PPO also converges fastest: median episodes remain low across all sweeps, while PPO and REINFORCE slow dramatically as conditions worsen. PPO’s clipping saturates under high-variance advantages, preventing meaningful policy updates. REINFORCE drifts randomly in parameter space, converging roughly half the time. With M=1M{=}1, ϕ\phi-PPO requires 2​T2T steps per episode (one counterfactual rollout), yielding 4×4{\times} episode efficiency but 2×2{\times} simulation efficiency over PPO.

E.2 Coin Flip MDP: High Stochasticity

A single-step MDP: U∼Bernoulli​(0.5)U\sim\text{Bernoulli}(0.5), action X∈{0,1}X\in\{0,1\}, return Y=100​U+XY=100U+X. The action’s causal effect is ϕ=1\phi=1 with zero variance, while Var⁡[Y]=2500\mathrm{Var}[Y]=2500. Correlation ρ=Corr⁡[Y⁡(0,U),Y⁡(1,U)]≈0.9998\rho=\mathrm{Corr}[Y(0,U),Y(1,U)]\approx 0.9998.

E.3 Treasure Hunt MDP: Delayed Reward

A T=4T=4 step MDP with terminal reward only. Each step: collect treasure or skip. Reward Y3=#​{collected}Y_{3}=\#\{\text{collected}\}. All actions are causal (k′=4k^{\prime}=4). ϕ\phi-TD provides signal in 1 episode; standard TD requires O⁡(T)=4O(T)=4 episodes for credit propagation.

Appendix F Limitations and Future Work

Scope.

Our approach requires a simulator to compute counterfactual trajectories, limiting applicability to environments with resettable state.

Limitations. Our approach requires simulator access for counterfactual trajectories. Sample complexity scales with σ2/(1−γ)2\sigma^{2}/(1-\gamma)^{2}, which can be large when γ≈1\gamma\approx 1. We assume counterfactual independence (Assumption 3.3), excluding correlated exogenous noise.

Future work. Finite-sample bounds via Bernstein concentration; relaxing counterfactual independence; empirical validation on Atari/MuJoCo benchmarks.

Appendix G Credit Assignment Methods: Detailed Comparison

To facilitate the discussion, here we entail the additional notations we use for related work comparison. αi→j\alpha_{i\to j}: learned attention weight from token jj to token ii. g(Δ0:t)g(\Delta_{0:t}): LSTM hidden state after processing trajectory up to step tt. Pπ​(Xt=x∣St,ST)P^{\pi}(X_{t}{=}x\mid S_{t},S_{T}): hindsight posterior over actions given a future state. Pπ​(Xt=x∣St,Z)P^{\pi}(X_{t}{=}x\mid S_{t},Z): hindsight posterior over actions given observed return ZZ. ϕ⋆​(s,x,z)\phi^{\star}(s,x,z): optimal DICE density-ratio estimator; χπ​(z∣s)\chi^{\pi}(z\mid s): return distribution under π\pi from state ss. Φt\Phi_{t}: learned hindsight statistic of the future trajectory, constrained to satisfy Xt⟂Φt|StX_{t}\perp\Phi_{t}\mid S_{t}. U′U^{\prime}: encoding of a future step (S′,X′,Y′)(S^{\prime},X^{\prime},Y^{\prime}); choices include U′=S′U^{\prime}{=}S^{\prime} (state), U′=Y′U^{\prime}{=}Y^{\prime} (reward), or a learned encoding. 𝒬⁡(s,x,τ)\mathcal{Q}(s,x,\tau): quantile function—inverse CDF of the return distribution Fηs,x−1​(τ)F^{-1}_{\eta_{s,x}}(\tau) at quantile level τ∈[0,1]\tau\in[0,1]. τ^\hat{\tau}: inferred quantile level of the observed return, τ^=FηSt,Xt​(Z)\hat{\tau}=F_{\eta_{S_{t},X_{t}}}(Z). Bπ(s,x,s′)=V(s′)−𝔼S′∼p(⋅|s,x)[V(S′)]B^{\pi}(s,x,s^{\prime})=V(s^{\prime})-\mathbb{E}_{S^{\prime}\sim p(\cdot|s,x)}[V(S^{\prime})]: luck (nature’s contribution to the transition).

First we provide an overview of the credit assignment methods we compare against in table 4 with their credit expressions and descriptions. Then table 5 evaluates each method against desirable credit assignment properties (3.1) on the Fork MDP (Section E.1: T=100T{=}100, σ=10\sigma{=}10, only X1X_{1} causal). Below we discuss the details of each category of credit assignment methods in the literature.

A. Temporal: discounted reward.

In the existing credit assignment literature, action values/advantages often serve as a key proxy for actions’ influence on the rewards (Watkins and Dayan, 1992; Sutton, 1988; Sutton et al., 1999; Schaul et al., 2015a; Sutton et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2021; Pan and Schölkopf, 2024; Auzina et al., 2026). Although action values and advantages yield unbiased gradients, they assign credit by actions’ temporal proximity to the reward, rather than their causal effects. This is both inefficient and biased in terms of credit assignment in that recent actions with no causal effect on the reward add noise to the gradient, while causally relevant actions that occur earlier receive discounted credit. Intuitively, credit should correspond to actions cause the outcome: we credit studying hard for a good grade, rather than flipping over the returned test to view the grade.

B. Memory: learned models

Another line of work utilizes learnable sequence models to automatically distribute the credit over actions (Chen et al., 2021; Arjona-Medina et al., 2019; Ferret et al., 2020; Raposo et al., 2021; Deng et al., 2026), dropping the reliance on the time contiguity assumption. However, such methods conflate agent’s actions influence over rewards with environment stochasticity. As a result, they are unable to distinguish skill from luck in learning. Also, learned models suffer from the same problem as black box models that they are also in lack of explainability.

C. Hindsight: posterior/prior ratios and conditional baselines

The line of hindsight conditioning (Harutyunyan et al., 2019a; Velu et al., 2024; Mesnard et al., 2021; Mesnard et al., 2023; Meulemans et al., 2023; Ramesh et al., 2025)22 2 For clarity, prior uses of the term ’counterfactual’ in this literature refer to hindsight conditioning not counterfactuals defined in the causal theory (Pearl, 2009). partially addresses the skill-luck issue by conditioning on future events and credit each action by how relevant it is to the given event. The fundamental limitation of those is that isolating each single action during attribution overlooks subsequent actions’ collective influence on the rewards. Thus, the skill-luck issue still persists as we demonstrate in Figure 1.
